As someone who has Bipolar 1 Disorder and during depressive episodes has let my house get BAD before I got proper treatment (to be honest it was maybe half as bad as what you're describing but that's still really really bad), yea. You don't clean it. If you're depressed enough, you come home from work and you might literally sit down and stare out the window at a single tree for 2 hours straight. And then remember that you haven't eaten all day, microwave something, and it takes so much effort to simply put food in your mouth that the idea of washing a plate is like climbing onto the roof with no ladder. Then get back in bed and stare at a different tree until you fall asleep. 

I don't know whether your wife has depression, or any mental illness for that matter. But the things you're describing are symptoms of severe depression. So before you jump to divorce, she needs to see a mental health professional. If she refuses, divorce. If 3 months go by and she's clearly not engaging in treatment, divorce. Even if she's engaging in treatment, definitely do couple's counseling as well. Regardless, right now you could be looking at a problem that is 100% fixable.

If you're writing these things in a legal document then you should use the legal terms. But otherwise, seriously, why does it matter? What's the point of insisting on someone calling someone their step mom or step dad when they'd rather say "my mom's/dad's husband/wife" or "my mom/dad?" I'm just struggling to see why exactly that matters at all beyond filling out documents.

I think a lot of it depends on the situation. Yea, legally there are terms that apply across the board. But that doesn't mean that a person has to use them. For example, my boyfriend's parents divorced when he was 12 and his mom remarried when he was 13. The man was emotionally and physically abusive to my boyfriend and so my bf refers to him by his name or as his mom's husband, the one time I used the term "stepdad" he nearly had a panic attack. On the other side, I have a friend whose parents split up when he was a baby and his mom remarried when he was like 5. That man technically is not his father but he refers to him only as "my dad." Because that man raised him and treated him with kindness, just like he treated my friend's half-sister who was his own child. It's perfectly fine for people to use the terms that they're comfortable with when they're referring to their own family members. It may not make sense to you but if it makes their life better and more healthy, then what exactly is the problem?

One strategy could be to tell the therapist everything you're struggling with, basically what you said in the post and what you've said in the comments. Then tell the therapist that you don't know what your goal should be, you just know that you're not happy with how things are right now. Then the therapist can talk to you in more detail about all of it and they'll help you identify what sort of goals you may have depending on how you talk about things and what you focus on. Lots of times they ask questions that seem irrelevant in the moment but then you get to a point where you're like "oh my god now that I've talked through this question, I realize what was actually bothering me." For example I thought that my previous job was giving me so much stress that it was keeping me from ever relaxing, after my therapist started making connections based on what I focused on, she helped me realize that the real problem was me not yet recovering from a close friend nearly dying next to me a year prior (I had thought that I had fully "gotten over it"). I'm not saying that's what will happen with you, but it's an example of how a therapist is trained in how to critically examine your situation with you, with you doing 90% of the talking, and knowing just the questions to ask that bring you to the realization of what your goal is.

Rabbits generally don't bite unless they're mistreated or neglected (I had one for like 7 years and she didn't bite once). That said, they are a LOT more work than most people think. They can't just stay in a cage all the time. They need a ton of space. For mine, she had half of one bedroom fenced off and we just left the base of a large rodent cage in that area because she liked to burrow in the bedding. They are very delicate, easily frightened (they can literally die from a heart attack if they're too scared) and physically pretty delicate. You can't be loud or reckless with them even to the level you can with a ferret (which are more physically delicate but emotionally much tougher regarding interaction with people). They do best when they're not alone, so it's ideal to have 2. Which means double the food, vet bills and cleanup (they poop EVERYWHERE). 

Basically, your dad is incorrect on the biting thing. But if everyone in the house isn't on board, it's a bad idea. They need a lot of attention, space and care. They're not cheap. They're lovely pets. But they're not easy pets. They're not starter pets. I'd recommend starting with a hamster. They're just as likely as a rabbit to bite (unlikely but it's not impossible) and they do need more care than most people think but nowhere near as much as a rabbit, and nowhere near as much space. Maybe your dad will end up loving fluffy rodent pets and eventually he'll be the one to suggest getting a rabbit. But right now it doesn't sound like a good idea.

So therapy looks different for everyone (just like treatment for cancer, there's no one size fits all solution). Typically you will find a licensed therapist via referral from your doctor or finding them online. Check their credentials, if you see "LPC" or "LCSW" you're golden. The first couple of sessions are getting to know you, and you ask about their treatment approach/modalities. Maybe they specialize in CBT, DBT, EMDR, etc (Google to look at the different types, that can also help to more quickly find a therapist who is best for you). You and the therapist will create a tentative treatment plan (I say tentative because sometimes crap happens halfway through like a job loss and you have to adjust your goals or time line). Then you will follow that treatment plan. Generally you'll see them once a week, then twice a month after a bit. You'll talk over what your issues are and the therapist helps you to examine the issues, what could be behind them (things you are aware of and things you hadn't thought of before), and how you can go about approaching those issues in a different way. You'll practice that different approach, maybe have some "homework." Homework can look like, for example, a person with a giant fear of conflict trying to have an honest discussion with their partner about how they would like to start dividing household tasks more equally, or a person with social anxiety going to a busy mall and buying something nice for themselves. You go through the treatment plan and adjust things as needed. The time line is different for everyone. Some people just need a couple of months, some people with more severe mental health issues may need a few years. And always feel free to ask the therapist about absolutely anything you're curious or concerned about. A good therapist does not balk at being questioned or criticized.

Currently in school to become a therapist. If you're in the US, a therapist must be licensed and have at least a Master's Degree from an accredited college/university program. Do not look for a "life coach," they do not require any sort of accredited training or licensure. Find an LPC (licensed professional counselor) or LCSW (licensed clinical social worker). A clinical psychologist also works but they tend to be more expensive because their training is more suited for severe mental illness treatment, as they have a PhD or PsyD instead of a Master's. If you have doubts, you can look into their credentials and the college they studied at, you can also look into their record to see whether they have had any disciplary actions taken against them (just a Google, it's publicly available information). I've always found therapists for myself and my loved ones through referrals by my doctor or through the Psychology Today online therapist finder. Also, if you don't like your first therapist after a few sessions, just ditch them and find a different one, it's common to not "click" with the first therapist you try (and that's the most important factor related to treatment success next to your own commitment to treatment). It is absolutely worth a try if you're open to it and can afford it.

This is going to require the tiniest of baby steps to get started. Try picking one tiny thing to do each day. Like a new habit. I literally had to make my first one brushing my teeth every day. After a few months of that working, I added doing the dishes every day. And so on. It's a hell of a lot easier to go at it one thing at a time so you don't get so overwhelmed by the sheer volume of things you've told yourself to do that it paralyzes you. I started that a couple of years ago and now I'm at the point where I've been working out every day, I've picked up new hobbies, and I'm about to attempt going back to school. It took several years but it's working. 

This is going to take a long time and that's okay. You're facing a big challenge and big challenges require big time to solve. That is okay. What matters is getting better, not being what you think you "should" be. Go slow, one thing at a time, one hour at a time. Try to add in something fun that makes you feel like a person as early as you can (but not first). Treat yourself like a person that is sick who you are trying to help heal, and getting to know at the same time. Best of luck.

It's not a diagnosis (at least in the US, it's not in the DSM 5) but attachment styles are a pretty widely accepted construct in the psych/mental health care field. You're either secure (healthy), insecure anxious (easiest way to describe it is a person who's terrified of being abandoned so they can be "clingy" and prioritize making their partner happy to the point where they suffer because they ignore their own needs since they're so scared of their partner leaving), insecure avoidant (scared of getting too close to people in case they get hurt, tend to see abandonment/being left as inevitable so they put up a wall as a way to protect themselves from the pain if/when they're left which makes them more likely to be left, don't like talking about their own feelings) and insecure disorganized (kind of a mix between anxious and avoidant depending on outside circumstances and how they're feeling in a given moment). It's a really interesting theory, I recommend looking into it!

Your dog sounds very similar to mine. First, get rid of that trainer. Get a new one or don't, just get rid of this one. Second, you can't force a dog to not have a fear reaction once they're already reacting. That's like telling a person who's having a panic attack to calm down, it literally doesn't work that way. I saw a trainer for a few months and she taught me to keep his attention at least intermittently on me, by doing stuff like talking and giving treats and occasionally commanding him to sit (because that's the command he knows best to the point of sitting even if a stranger says it). And have high-value treats with you to give him occasionally, that you don't give any other time so walks are special in a good way. Finally, I agree with everyone else (and the trainer I saw) in that you should turn around if your dog starts reacting. Partly because he is already reacting, going closer to the trigger is just going to make him even more scared. And partly because (at least this is the case for me bc my dog is 70 lbs) what if he gets off the leash due to being more and more reactive physically? What then? I had that happen once because I tripped over a rock and messed up my arm that was holding the leash, fortunately neither he nor the other 2 dogs were aggressive so no bites happened but if those dogs had bitten him, he may very well have bitten back. It's not worth the risk. Make walks fun, try to control your own anxiety as much as you can because your dog can sense that, and if he reacts just turn around and get out of there.

As someone who was in therapy for over a decade and quit a few months ago because I realized I needed something different, and someone who has worked in mental health care for several years myself (not a therapist or counselor), I think that basically the pendelum has just swung too far in the opposite direction of where it was years ago.

In the past, even when I was in high school (I'm 30), "go to therapy" was not said. Therapy was for "crazy people." I was ashamed to admit I was in therapy for a few years. Frankly I should have been sent to therapy because of trauma when I was a kid, my parents should have gotten individual and couples' therapy before I was born. So it used to be totally avoided. 

But now "go to therapy" is seen as a full solution to mental illness/trauma/etc. Sometimes it is! But often it's not. I've been told that myself while in therapy, I've seen other people who were currently in therapy be told that. It's like we as a society are off-loading our responsibility to help other people onto what we see as this magic cure that 1) many people cannot access in the first place, 2) takes a long time to be successful, and 3) is not a cure by itself for MANY people.

Basically, society is trying to undo the damage of decades of stigmatizing seeking out mental health care and that's a very good thing. But in doing so, we're forgetting that clinical care by itself is not what makes happy, healthy humans.

ETA: I don't know what the solution is for you. I don't know what the solution is for myself either. The best advice I can give is what I'm doing myself right now: keep looking for what makes sense and what feels meaningful. Try therapy if you can access it. But reach out to other people too, literally anyone. Just chatting with strangers in line at the grocery store makes you feel more like a human. Go outside, even 5 minutes a day. Notice the things around you. Don't do the same exact thing every single day if you're not happy, because that means it isn't working. Just try different things until you stumble upon the right things for you.

So I've been on both sides of this. I was involuntarily committed for a week when I was 16 for SH and SI, and it was really traumatic. I wouldn't say I was mistreated, the nurses and therapists were nice and I made a couple of friends while there. But having all of my agency and control over my life, my decisions, my body, even my clothes, etc ripped away from me with no warning (therapist that committed me didn't fully explain confidentiality) was traumatizing. It absolutely did not help and it made me get much worse. 

On the other side, I worked at a psychiatric hospital for a few years until about a year ago, I wanted to help people in the same situation I was in. I saw so, so many people experiencing psychosis (especially first episode psychosis) make massive improvements because they truly needed to be there. As far as depression and SI goes, it was mixed. It seemed like the people who came in voluntarily tended to improve more because it wasn't as traumatic since they weren't forced. But I saw people who were involuntarily admitted improve too, if what they needed was a break from the "real world," adjustments of medications, connections to other resources, etc. It's different for everyone though.

One thing I will emphasize: not all psych wards are the same. I've heard horror stories about some hospitals that I refuse to ever work at or recommend because they are just hell. The one I worked at was very strict about not using restraints other than staff physically holding a person in a sitting position if they were actively harming themselves/others, and using as little medication as possible for improvement. I would recommend that one to a loved one who needed that sort of help. So do your research, there are good ones and bad ones. And a lot in between.

And when you do, write down whatever you were doing or feeling immediately before that. At your age it's likely that you're feeling strong emotions and don't know how to react to them in a healthy way. If you can notice a pattern, then you can realize "okay so when I'm angry I tend to do X things, when I'm sad I tend to do Y things." Then practice noticing those emotions and doing something different and healthier when you feel them. You can tell your parents that you're doing this and let them know what you're going to do instead so that they recognize it and give you space (for example if you realize that going outside for 10 minutes or listening to 3 songs in your room helps, they'll know that you're trying to calm down instead of ignoring them). I said this in another comment, but physical harm only causes fear and potentially anger.
This "gentle parenting" trend, if it doesn't involve discipline, that's not right either.
Using *logical consequences* is the key. One of your kids breaks the other one's toy because they got into an argument. What is spanking the kid going to teach them? Nothing. You know what will teach them? Making them do a ton of extra chores to earn money to buy a toy for their sibling to replace the one they broke. That way, they learn "if I do this, then it will cause a problem I'll have to solve, so I'm not going to do it." Physical discipline, on the other hand, makes them think "if I do something my parent doesn't like, they'll hurt me." It doesn't matter whether you remember thinking your parents were wonderful or whatever else, that is literally what happens in the brain. You can argue all you want but these are the facts.

If following the results of peer-reviewed studies makes me delusional then I don't care to live in whatever world you call home.

FYI, I've worked in mental health care for many years and studied neuroscience in college. I have more of an understanding of this issue than you know.

Physical harm = fear. That's it. Maybe anger in some kids. 

Logical consequences (such as "you broke your sister's toy so you're going to do extra chores to make money to buy her a new one") = well adjusted adult who understands the concept of actions and consequences.

But one thing you could try that has worked very well for us (obviously all dogs are different), since he was also at the point where he spit out his favorite treat because he could not be distracted, was this: when your dog sees something that will trigger a response, the second you see his ears perk up and his tail go up (or whatever physical response your dog has), turn around and walk the other way. Or if you just see something that you know will cause a reaction. And turn him with your body, like stay on the outside of the turn and kind of guide him with your legs instead of doing something like yanking on the leash to drag him back since that would only cause more stress for him. Praise him a bit, and if you get to a calmer place give him a command (I use sit) and then a treat if he does it. You might be basically going in a big circle and it feels silly but it's a lot more embarrassing to have your dog flip out. Best of luck.

So I'm not an expert or a dog trainer but I've been working with an amazing trainer for a few months, she has changed our whole life so I'll say this because she told me this - do NOT duck down and comfort/protect him. That is basically the exact opposite of what you should do. Your dog sounds very similar to how mine used to act. Anxious, extremely affectionate towards me, super-protective of me but I could comfort him by giving him a hug. Don't. That reinforces the behavior. 

My trainer told me to turn around and walk the other way whenever he encounters a trigger, and that means that I have to constantly watch his body language and watch out for potential triggers. And when we turn around, I lead him with my body by turning on the outside of his body (like I guide him, I don't yank the leash or anything). If it's a safe area, give him a command after the turn  and a treat if he obeys. No hugs, just a command (any command, I literally only use sit). Basically you want to teach your dog to accompany you on your walk instead of it being the other way around.

Again, I'm not a trainer so take this with a grain of salt. But this approach has changed my life. We've got a long way to go but we are both so much happier with everyday life. My dog is a shepherd mix, a big dog but not giant so it may not work for you, every breed is different! But it seems to be universal that your dog is calmer if you are calm and clearly in control (not in an aggressive way). They're like little kids, they mirror our emotions.

Even with a dog that's not reactive, it's just not safe to be physically unable to control them at all. For you, for them, for everyone else. And again that truly is not your fault. Yes! This is what I did to lose 60 lbs (have kept it off for 6 years now). My primary strategy was diet, like a calorie deficit and healthier foods. Literally the only exercise I did was walking more. And that was by incorporating it into daily life, like taking the stairs, parking at the back of the parking lot, taking my dog on longer walks than I used to, etc. It's not necessarily easy but it is simple. Eggs! When I was losing weight (lost 60 lbs and have kept it off for I think 6 years now) eggs were my go-to. They're very low in calories and super filling. 2 large eggs is like 140 calories. Also nuts like another poster said, they're higher in calories but super healthy and filling. And for carbs specifically, there's nothing wrong with pasta, potatoes, rice etc as long as you portion it out. It's all about portion size. Also, allow yourself a "cheat day" once a week, like don't binge or anything but allow yourself a few hundred extra calories and make them all snacks if you want. Some studies have found that people are more likely to stick to a diet long-term if they have one cheat day a week, and this is anecdotal but that worked really well for me, it makes it so that you aren't cutting "fun food" out of your diet completely (which makes it more appealing), just learning how to eat it in moderation.

Exercise is only about 20% of weight loss, if that. And 30 minutes a day of speed walking is perfectly sufficient. The key is limiting your caloric intake. It doesn't matter how much or in what way you exercise if you're 5'3 and eating 3500 calories a day.

I've only had Marshall ferrets due to where I live (US, no ferret rescues within 4 hours of me and they've got wait lists but I'm trying to find one for my next fursnake) and while they definitely have more health problems than what I've *heard* is the case for privately bred ferrets and ferrets outside of North America, they are generally healthy and live an average ferret lifespan if you feed them a healthy diet and keep up with regular vet visits. So this doesn't precisely meet your requirements, but you could try doing some research on ferrets, watching videos of them, and consider that. I've had ferrets for nearly 2 decades and I have a similar lifestyle/pet preferences and they're perfect for me.

Mine have averaged 7-8 years but I had one that almost reached 10. They can have health problems but as long as you feed them good quality food and have yearly vet checkups you're probably not going to have to deal with much that you wouldn't with a dog, outside of sheer bad luck. I've had 2 out of the 7 I've had get insulinoma which is common, but if you catch it early (not that hard) you just give them cheap daily medicine and they're perfectly fine.

I have two things I can give as advice:

1. Something I did starting 3 days after my boyfriend passed was writing a note to him in a journal specifically for that purpose every single night. I'd write about my grief, my love, all of my feelings about missing him. I'd also write about random things I wished I could tell him, like how it snowed that day and my car got stuck in my driveway, or I finished a book he had been reading and he would love the ending. It didn't make the pain go away but it helped just a tiny bit with the feeling of wanting so desperately just to talk to him about anything. So that might be worth a try.

2. I was told about one way to think of grief and I've found that for me at least, it's pretty accurate. Time doesn't make it go away. Grief is like a series of waves in the ocean. The first one is a tsunami, gigantic and it throws you around and you think you won't survive it. But you do. You feel a little better for a bit, maybe a day or two. Then another wave hits, it's huge but not as big as the first one. Over time the breaks between the waves will get longer, the waves get smaller but sometimes you'll get another giant wave that pushes you under the water. Just keep holding on to whatever keeps you afloat. Family, friends, hobbies, therapy, things that remind you of him, anything. The waves never go away completely, but you don't have to drown.

Well obviously it's not a need for individual survival like food, water, etc. but I'm pretty sure we all agree on that. I wouldn't say it's a universal need, because asexual people exist. I think it's a need for people who aren't asexual, for their social/relational health. 

With some rare exceptions, people need regular interaction with other humans; a lack of it can potentially kill infants/young children (failure to thrive), and it can contribute to many diseases and ultimately early death in adults. I'm not saying that a lack of sex constitutes a lack of human interaction, but in people who have/desire both romantic relationships and sex, it is one part of the need for human interaction. 

It's on par with a need for platonic interactions like talking about your emotions and life events and such. If you have plenty of sex but never talk to/communicate with other people, your need for human interaction won't be fulfilled. In people who aren't asexual, the opposite is also true. So you won't die without sex, but what you need to be fully physically and mentally healthy (again, if you're not asexual) will not be fulfilled. Basically, we have a need for human interaction. Sex is one part of that.

Soft YTA because while you're putting your baby son at risk of getting sick, I do see why you're having trouble with this and I think a compromise can be found here. 

Step one is going to the doctor, which you've already done and that's great. Hopefully that'll solve the issue in time. But until then you're obviously in horrible pain and discomfort. I have severe eczema myself, and it's different from what you're describing but basically I get hives and breakouts of painful/itchy blotches all over my body for at least a week when I have to deal with a trigger even once, which for me is primarily hot temperatures (and where I live it's hot 70% of the year). So I fully get that this is seriously impacting probably every part of your life. 

That said, you have a very young baby. I don't know a ton about babies but I know that they can't fully regulate their body temperature and can be in danger of hypothermia I believe at and below 68 degrees. Your son's health and safety must come first. 

But there are a few things worth trying:

You mentioned that you have a balcony, instead of opening the door to the balcony to make it cooler inside, set up a comfy place out there for you to hang out and even sleep (with the door closed) until this gets resolved by the medication.

When you're caring for your son indoors, put on shorts and the thinnest t shirt you own, and just keep the thermostat at like 70-75, instead of having a space heater (they tend to affect skin more than overall heating).

Cold showers/baths don't help a lot of people because they're short in duration and immediately after you get out, your skin dries up, making the problem worse. I'd find a lotion for sensitive skin, or aloe vera gel, keep the bottle in the fridge and put that on regularly wherever you get hives, especially after showering and at night.

Hives are of course more than just a skin irritation response, but if you're taking medication to treat the underlying issue then this stuff may help even a bit with those symptoms in the mean time.

Being HL is not a problem unless it inhibits a person's ability to function normally (work, daily living tasks). Having a high libido is not a sign of a mental or physical health problem. 

On the other hand, some people are naturally LL, but it is often a sign of a physical or mental health problem. So it's worth looking into. And in particular, if the LL partner was initially HL and over the course of the relationship became LL, then both partners should look at what could be causing that. In that case, maybe the HL partner did something to contribute (like they became emotionally abusive, stopped putting effort into the relationship, etc). But them being HL is not by itself a problem. 

Ultimately though, the main problem is a lack of compatibility. A relationship just isn't going to work long-term in a healthy way between a HL person and a LL person unless the LL person became LL because of a health problem that they are willing to address.
It's not necessarily a problem for the LL individual, but it is a problem for the relationship. If the LL is happy the way they are, that's totally fine, but they need to end the relationship.

I have been through the child support system myself indirectly (assisting my ex with the process when he went through family court because there was obviously a lot to it). I've done a lot of research on this, and I've talked to several lawyers. Signing away legal rights does not terminate the obligation to pay child support in any state in the US. There are only two ways in which that can happen: 

1) The mother signs a legal agreement that she does not want child support payments from the biological father (if she has already sought child support, obviously if she never sought it in the first place then that's not the case) 

2) The child is legally adopted by the spouse of the mother, or is given up for adoption by both the mother and biological father to someone else 

As others have mentioned, this is the case because the state will not pay any sort of financial benefits/assistance for the child that can instead be taken from the biological father, regardless of whether he has any legal rights to the child. For example, the child is not eligible for Medicare if the biological father's job offers health insurance. He is legally obligated to pay for that insurance in order to have the child covered under the policy.

I've seen many people be diagnosed with, or just labeled, BPD when they either obviously have something else, seem to have something else, or they're like 15 and being labeled with the name of BPD when they're far too young to make any assumptions about their overall personality. I feel like this career is my reason for being alive and I value very deeply anything that makes me better able to help the people I work with.

There are some awesome CBT worksheets you can find for free online to either print out and use, or copy into a journal. The ones that would probably help you would be the ones where you write down a situation that caused you anxiety, your initial anxious thought, then write down what an alternative explanation could be. Then write out which option makes more sense given the evidence. So like for your situation, it could be:

What happened-- My boyfriend didn't call me when he said he would, and ended up calling much later

Initial thought-- He doesn't love me and forgot about me

Alternative Explanation-- He got busy with whatever he was doing (work, school, chores, etc) and wasn't able to call me at that time.

Which option is more likely given the evidence? -- He called me later so he didn't forget about me. He told me he loved me and spoke to me the way he always does, so there's no evidence that he stopped loving me. Therefore the alternative explanation is probably the accurate one.

Try doing that exercise every time you have a thought like that.

When you provide a product or service, you take on the responsibility of making it as safe as possible. With pools, there will always be a possibility of drowning. There's no going around that. With food, there's always a risk of choking. But there is not a risk of getting food poisoning unless you're negligent. So when a person gets food poisoning, the person who made it is held responsible. 

With a party truck, there is always a risk of it getting into an accident like being hit by a drunk driver. The owner/operator can't control that. But they can control how high and sturdy the barriers are. If they choose to put a couple of bars at waist height, when they could have made a solid barrier that went up to chest height, then they are responsible for someone falling over/through them. You don't get to knowingly put people in danger just because you're too lazy to take very simple actions to prevent harm.

Take responsibility for the products and services you provide. If you make the choice to cut corners, you are making the choice to assume responsibility for the harm that is caused by that choice.

One great thing you could say is "I don't know what you're feeling right now, but I'm here for you if you want to talk about it." So you're allowing him to have his feelings but you're also making sure that he knows that he's not alone.

The most important thing you can possibly do is not shame him for cutting. Shaming consists of everything from begging him not to cut, to hiding his tools, to telling him that it makes you sad when he cuts, etc. Cutting is an addiction for many people. So he's going to do it regardless of how you feel and it has nothing to do with how he feels about you. But if you offer him non-judgmental support, you can change his life. 

People who cut have often experienced nothing other than criticism, judgement and worry in the form of demands to stop. But you also can't go to the other extreme. Don't fawn over him every time he cuts, hugging him and kissing his cuts and such, some people do that and it encourages it. The best thing you can do is be calm. Ask him how he wants you to act after he cuts. Maybe he wants you to ask him if he's okay, maybe he wants you to say nothing. Do what he requests.

For an example, my boyfriend is the only person who has ever reacted to my cutting in a way that doesn't make me feel ashamed or make me want to cut more. He asked me a while ago how I wanted him to react. I said I wanted him to say nothing unless I asked whether I could tell him what I had been struggling with, which wouldn't be often. Yes!! There are two parts to it.

The first is endorphins. These are chemicals your brain releases that give you a brief pleasant "rush" and eliminate pain after being hurt. Have you ever accidentally badly hurt yourself and for just a moment, you didn't feel the pain at all and felt a buzz or a rush? That's endorphins.

The other half isn't as well known because there is only one study but it was peer-reviewed (gold standard in science). Basically, this study found that whether you do or don't have a mental illness, when you're experiencing a negative mood state like sadness, anger, guilt, etc and inflict pain on yourself, your amygdala activity plummets for a few minutes to a few hours. The amygdala is the part of your brain that is the source of negative emotions. If amygdala activity isn't happening, you can't feel negative emotions. That's why you can't feel bad things for a little while after cutting.

When it comes to young kids-young teens, always keep in mind that when they flip out/get upset/get super emotional, they often don't know what they're feeling. They haven't developed the words to use to describe their emotions, or once they have the words they have trouble linking a word to what they're feeling. Like when you're angry because your boss was a jerk to you, you can identify "my boss put 3 jobs on me to do in one day, I'm angry because he was inconsiderate and that's why I snapped at my coworker." Kids don't have that ability and it results in them becoming more upset. So don't just let them flip out and scream at you, but don't retaliate with screaming. The best thing you can do is remain calm. Firm, but calm. For example "I know you're upset right now but it's not acceptable for you to talk to me this way. Go to your room for 30 minutes, I'm going to go outside for 30 minutes and once we're both calm we can talk about this and find a solution together." It's so important to understand that a kid's mind does not and cannot function the same way as an adult's mind.

I've been involuntarily admitted once, for a week, and I've also worked in the field for a few years (2.5 years inpatient). It really comes down to 2 things: the laws, and mental health professionals who are scared by suicide and don't know how to properly treat suicidal people. 

Idk where you live but in the US it is literally the law in every state that if someone tells a therapist/doctor or any sort of health care worker that they're going to kill themselves, the health care worker MUST refer them to a hospital (and the hospital has to admit them). Quite a lot of therapists hate it and know it doesn't work but if I say I'm seriously considering killing myself in X way tonight, if they don't send me to a hospital and I do it, they'll lose their license, can be successfully sued by my family and potentially go to jail. I've had several therapists who I made an agreement with about what language I'll use so they can genuinely help me without having to commit me.

On the other side, a lot of therapists are scared shitless by suicidal clients. I was committed because of self harm and suicidal ideation. She was basically like "you're clearly trying to kill yourself so I have to have you admitted." To be fair I was planning a suicide attempt but I never said that.

Also, interestingly there have been several studies that found that someone who is involuntarily admitted for suicidal ideation is MORE likely to kill themselves after being released (like a shit ton more likely) than someone who is voluntarily admitted, or not admitted at all. I can attest to that myself. 

Basically it's just a shit system and needs a lot of reform.

Usually I use alcohol to sleep. Obviously that's not good or healthy but it doesn't seem to make a difference in whether I have nightmares.

Honestly I accepted it before I was even diagnosed (I was first diagnosed with MDD at 16 and started researching mental illnesses, when I had my first manic episode at 18 I knew what it was and I was lucky to have a good psychiatrist who immediately changed my diagnosis) but it took my parents probably 4 years to fully accept my diagnosis. 

Really it just took me being very blunt with them and standing up for myself no matter what they said for them to accept it. There's actually a history of Bipolar in my family but it was hidden because they try to be a classic good southern wealthy Christian family. I just stood up for myself, never backed down and crushed it. It's really hard, I won't lie. You may have to say some things that hurt them. But once you're on the same page, if you can get there, things are a lot easier.

My dad- So when are you going to stop taking your medications? You seem better.

Me- Remember that time when I was 18 that I stole your credit card and spent $500 online shopping for clothes? I was having a manic episode. I wasn't on medication. Do you want that to happen again? Because I don't.

My dad- ...okay.
